Manal’s eyes flicked sideways toward the door. “Noted. No blended.”

He exhaled. “I guess it’s just about keeping the peace. Though not everyone agrees what peace looks like.”

She tilted her head. “Peace is a spectrum. For some it’s silence, for others it’s proximity. You’re writing the map, not the destination.”

Gideon tapped his pen. “So if I write ‘a complicated but meaningful chapter,’ does that cover the silence and the holidays?”

“Try ‘a shared history that shaped each of us differently.’ That lets readers fill in their own blanks.”

He wrote it down, then paused. “What about the son who left and never came back? Do I even mention him?”

Manal’s pen stilled. “Only if he asks to be. If not, leave space. Omission can be respectful too.”

Gideon nodded slowly. “Thanks, Manal. You make grief sound almost manageable.”

She smiled faintly. “It’s just words. But sometimes words are the only bridge left.”

Manal’s lips twitched. “Noted. No blended. One friend told me they got the call from their cousin that their aunt had passed while she was still watching a movie about a blended family. Said the irony hit like a freight train. So yeah, I keep it clean.”

Gideon exhaled, shoulders dropping. “Thanks. I just don’t want to accidentally hurt anyone. Some of us still feel like we’re waiting for an invitation that never comes.”

She nodded. “That’s why the order matters. Names first. Then the framing. It’s not about erasing; it’s about giving everyone a seat without forcing them to sit in one.”

He glanced at the draft again, already feeling lighter. “What about the part where I mention he was ‘always there’? My stepdad wasn’t. But I don’t want to sound bitter.”

“Then don’t say ‘always there.’ Say ‘present during key milestones.’ Or leave it out entirely. You’re not obligated to celebrate every version of a family.”

Gideon smiled faintly. “You make it sound so simple. But it’s not, is it?”

Manal leaned against the doorframe, eyes softening. “No, it’s not. But you don’t have to carry the whole history in one paragraph. Just tell the truth you can live with.”

“Got it.” He clicked twice and the spreadsheet opened. “I only see one column.”

Esme leaned in. “You opened the wrong sheet. The one called Redirects.” She tapped his shoulder, a quick tap designed to mean *I’m here*, not *You’re in the way*.

He exhaled, which meant he was thinking again. “Can I just do this in my head?”

“Not today,” Esme said, but she smiled anyway. “Today we use the grid preview so you can see what breaks before it breaks for everyone else.”

He typed the first row: `/old/blogs/2023/05/penguins-and-pie` → `/news/2023/05/penguins-and-pie`. The preview grid flickered green. “Okay, that one lived.”

“Good. Keep going. I’ll watch for duplicates.”

They worked in the rhythm of two people who had learned not to interrupt each other’s cadence. Viktor’s keys sounded like rain; Esme’s eyes moved in steady left-to-right sweeps. A few rows in, he hit a snag. “This one’s got a trailing slash. Does the plugin care?”

“Sometimes. If the page was originally without slash and now is with, it’ll 404. Put a note in the comments column and we’ll fix it after publish.”

“Understood,” he said, and his smile was the polite kind that meant he’d done it anyway.

Esme’s own project was a small one: a landing page for a community mapping workshop. She’d built it on the same server, but the theme’s style sheet was stubborn. The background stayed white in the editor, yet on the front end it rendered the color of dried milk. She’d already checked if she’d forgotten to set the body background, which she hadn’t.

“Can you look at my page?” she asked. “The background won't take.”

Viktor leaned over her shoulder. He smelled like coffee and the faint metal of solder. “Did you try refreshing?”

“I’ve done that. Twenty times.”

He scrolled slowly. The page was clean, the grid neat, the font choices deliberate. But the white background was a wall. “What’s the theme name again?”

“Twenty Twenty-Five.”

“Minimalist, right?”

“Minimal to the point of cruelty.”

He opened the theme folder, then the functions.php file. “Wait—do you have a child theme?”

“Yeah, but I don’t know what that means.”

Viktor’s eyebrows climbed. “You should create one. If you don’t, any update to Twenty Twenty-Five wipes out your edits. You lose your custom CSS, your modified templates. All of it.”

Pippa’s mouth twitched. “Wouldn’t dream of it. Try the pause for five reps. Audio capture it.”  

They set up a phone on a stack of playbills. Octavio ran the cycle twice more, then on the third he lingered. The ball hung. The room seemed to hold its breath. The catch snapped back into rhythm.  

He exhaled. “Okay. That actually felt bigger. Also, weirdly satisfying.”  

Pippa nodded. “Now let’s talk about what you’re doing with the crowd work. You’ve been dodging the ‘quick question’ bit again.”  

Octavio’s shoulders dropped. “It’s fine. I’m fine. The bit is fine. Why do I keep skipping it?”  

“Because it’s unscripted. You like control. Same reason you won’t try the pause until I drew a timeline on the whiteboard.”  

He rubbed his neck, smile crooked. “Fair.”  

“Pick one question you’d ask an imaginary person in row four. Something you’re curious about right now.”  

He looked up at the chalk dust motes drifting in the stage light. “Do you ever wonder if you’re just rehearsing the same mistake in different costumes?”  

Silence settled, comfortable. Pippa capped the marker. “Good question. You’ll ask it after the second ball crosses your left shoulder. Pause. Ask. Then catch.”

Pippa slid the clipboard onto a bench. “No torches. Try a light cue. Hit the final catch exactly when the house lights dip.” She tapped the clipboard again. “Do you want safe or do you want standing ovation?”  

Octavio stared at the beanbags, each one slightly scuffed at the equator. Safe meant six more weeks of identical sets, identical nods, identical checks that paid the rent but never bought the ticket to the next city. Standing ovation meant people would remember his name, or at least the shape it made in the air.  

He picked up the three balls. “What if I miss the dip?”  

“You’ll look like you’re dancing with the lights. Better than looking like you’re apologizing for them.”  

Octavio let the balls roll through his palms, cold and familiar. He set them on his shoulder, one each, then flicked them into the arc. He counted the beats under his breath and, on the last throw, held it just a hair longer than comfort allowed. The gym’s overhead fluorescents flickered, unnoticed by anyone else, but Octavio felt the tiny gap widen like a breath.  

He caught the ball and exhaled. “I’ll try it Friday.”  

Pippa nodded, already scribbling. “Good. And Octavio?”  

“Yeah?”

"Noted." She pressed a folded flyer into his palm. "Press it against the corner where it meets the rail. If the tape stays tacky, it'll slide like a sled. If it sticks, it'll act as a brake. Either way, no gouges."

He breathed in the sharp tang of old paper and the faint chemical sweetness that hung in the stairwell air. "You make it sound like a physics problem."

"It is," she said, smiling. "Mass, friction, and the courage to lean."

He nodded, adjusted his grip, and set his shoulder to the oak again. Below them, the city exhaled—a distant siren, a car door, a dog’s brief bark through a cracked window. The banister waited, patient as a judge. Bashir felt the weight of the bookcase settle into his bones, and for a moment, the world narrowed to the angle of the wood, the grit of the paint, and the steady presence of someone who knew exactly how to make the impossible move one degree at a time.

"Ready?" he asked.

"Ready," she said. "Tilt. Pivot. Breathe."

They moved together. The oak scraped, sighed, and cleared the rail by a fraction of an inch, the laminated flyer singing softly against the paint. Bashir exhaled. Eulalia’s coffee stayed level.

"Right," she said, smiling, "keep the acetone away from the finish."

He set his shoulder to the bookcase, felt the oak bite into his jacket, and pushed. "On three—one, two—"

"Wait," she said, stopping him with a finger on the frame. "Sweep the landing first. There’s a throw rug under that stack of magazines; if the edge catches, the whole thing drops like a stage prop."

He crouched and dragged the rug aside. "Thanks. I wouldn’t want the whole thing to drop like a stage prop."

They tried again. The bookcase tilted, the lower corner caught, the top edge kissed the rail, and Bashir’s shoulder screamed. "Okay, okay—easy." He exhaled, shifted his weight, and the piece pivoted. The banister groaned but held. "You were right about the angle."

"Was it?" she asked, already peeling the coupon flyer to reveal a hidden flyer for a free trial of something nobody needed. "Or was it just gravity doing what it does?"

"Both," he said. "Now, tell me again how you move a grand piano without a forklift."

She laughed, the sound bouncing off the peeling peach paint. "You don’t. You hire someone who knows how to weld a dolly to the floor and pray the building’s bones are stronger than the piano’s pride."

Javed stopped mid-sentence, blinked, then let out a breathy laugh. “Nope. Noted. I’ll stick to a custom rsync script I wrote.”

“Is that the one I’m supposed to ask about?”

He grinned. “You got me. But it’s clean. I’ll show you.”

She typed faster, the terminal output scrolling like rain. “You know, for a guy who spends half his life hiding data, you’re pretty friendly about it.”

“Only because you’re asking the right questions.” He leaned back, chair creaking. “Also—your laptop’s fan sounds like a jet engine.”

“It’s fine. It’s just working hard.”

“Yeah. Me too.” 

For a beat, the only sound was the clack of keys and the hum of drives. Outside, a car door slammed. They didn’t look up.

Javed blinked, then burst out laughing, a warm sound that seemed to loosen the tightness in his shoulders. “Noted. No Bacula. I’ll stick to my script and a simple archive-and-move.”

“Exactly. Keep it simple.”

They worked in comfortable silence for a while, the hum of the server fans filling the gaps. When the copy finally finished, Javed leaned back. “You’re good at this. Most people just delete everything they don’t understand.”

Hannelore smiled, small and genuine. “I’ve learned the hard way that audits don’t care about understanding. They care about consistency. And this way,” she tapped the screen, “we both sleep better.”

“True. Hey—” He hesitated, then dug into his backpack and pulled out a slightly squashed paper bag. “I brought coffee. And, uh, cookies. In case you needed a break.”

She looked at the bag, then at him. “You don’t have to bribe me with baked goods, Javed.”

“I know. But I like them, and you look like you could use one.” He slid a cookie across the table. It was still warm.

She took a bite. It was perfect. “Thanks.”

He grinned, pulling up his own terminal. “Anytime. Now, about that exclude-list—”

Tariq’s eyes crinkled. "Lifted the entire bezel off?"

"It was a teacup; the whole thing exploded."

He grinned, unrepentant. "Well, you didn’t use a capillary tube then. Controlled flow, no splash."

Giselle pursed her lips. "You’re offering to help, right? Or just to watch me fail?"

"Help. But I’m dictating: needle vent, epoxy, flush shave, no cyano. I’ll hand you syringes full of thinned epoxy and a fresh scalpel."

She huffed, but there was no heat in it. "Deal. And if it lifts, I’m telling everyone you sabotaged it."

"Fair."

They worked in tight tandem, fingers brushing over the bench as he measured, mixed, and handed her tools before she asked. The epoxy set, the needle carved a breath of escape for the enamel, and the single edge came down in one clean pass. The chip vanished, leaving only a shine where the new clay met the old.

Giselle tilted the pin toward the light. "Looks clean."

"Looks like you did it alone," Tariq said, already gathering his iron.

She slid the pin into a box. "Next time, you’re making the mistake."

He laughed, low and warm. "Deal. But I’m using a capillary tube."

Tariq lifted his hands in gentle surrender. "Noted. PVA then. Thin mix, brush on, cure, scrape. You'll keep the detail and avoid the flash."

She exhaled, the tension leaving her shoulders in one long breath. "You're a lifesaver."

He shrugged, smiling at the floor. "Not me. You. You just have to listen to me."

Ulric’s laugh was a low, warm thing. “Deal. We’ll use Freight Text Pro—clean, modern, and it won’t make the strawberry jam look like a cartoon.”

She hit print. The first sheet slid into the tray, crisp and true. The jars waited, gleaming under the fluorescent hum, no longer bleeding, no longer uncertain—just ready for the bake sale’s crowded tables.

“Obviously. Try Garamond or a clean sans like Helvetica Neue. The jar’s mouth becomes the visual center, so keep the text small enough to let the fruit speak.”

She typed, then paused. “What about a white stroke around the text so it isn’t lost in the red?”

“Good instinct. Two-point stroke, 50% opacity. It’ll float without shouting.”

Whitney nudged the sample jar closer. “You’re the reason these labels don’t end up looking like ransom notes.”

Ulric’s mouth curved, just barely. “I’m the reason they don’t look like ransom notes. You’re the reason they actually match the jars.”

She pulled the first sheet from the feeder. The labels sat crisp, the red pulp dots feathered softly, the text riding tidy ovals. No bleeding. No measles.

“Perfect,” she said.

“Close enough for a bake sale,” Ulric replied, already reaching for the next sheet. “Now, about the lemon curd…”

“Understood.” She typed with her left hand and held the scanner with her right, a one-handed juggling act against the fluorescent hum. “I’ll flag your account to prevent automatic mail-order enrollment. Any other preferences?”

“Just that I’d like the new pharmacy to call when it’s ready. Texts get buried.”

“Noted.” She hit submit, then leaned forward as if sharing a secret. “Here’s what’s going to happen: I’m adding Maple Leaf as your primary location. The switch is active immediately. Next time you log into the portal, you’ll see ‘Primary Pharmacy: Maple Leaf on 34th.’ If you ever need to revert, you can ask here or call the new pharmacy.”

Claudio exhaled a laugh he hadn’t planned. “That’s… suspiciously simple.”

Nyla’s smile stretched, genuine. “It’s a two-minute update. We do it all the time.”

He tapped his card against the scanner again, more for rhythm than necessity, and watched the little green light swallow the transaction. Through the plexi, the pharmacy hummed on—counters, printers, the soft thud of bottles sliding into brown paper—which suddenly felt less like a waiting room and more like a place where things just worked.

“Understood.” She tapped a checkbox that read Mail-Order Opt-Out. “You’re all set. I’ll print a confirmation slip with the new routing info for your records.”

She slid the paper through the slot. The pill pen stopped dancing. For a moment, the pharmacy was just a room again—fluorescent, quiet, waiting for the next person who needed somewhere better to send their future.

“Noted. No lavender.”

She turned to the scale, already dialing back clove, ready to build the cone properly.

“Noted.” He finally looked up, sleeves rolled, eyes bright. “You’re close. The warmth is there; you’re just fighting it instead of letting it lead.”

She smiled, mixing until the blend looked like uniform sand. “Then I’ll stop wrestling and start conducting.”

“I didn't see any premium profiles,” Jericho says smoothly. “Did you?”

Yuna blinks. “There it is. You totally saw it. You're not supposed to know about those.”

“I know the menu; I don't know the billing profile. Different departments. I'm just here to make the labels survive rain and candle wax.” He taps the queue. “See? Eight-color is grayed out. We're in the standard black-and-white night mode. You're good.”

Yuna exhales, shoulders dropping a degree. “Okay. I'll prep the PDFs. If it says ‘premium’ again, I'm walking.”

“Fair.” He grins. “Next time, I'll wear a tie and carry a clipboard. It helps.”

Outside, the campus bells strike midnight. Inside, the VS-540 purrs, and fifty cream circles begin to take shape, precise as breath.

He laughs. “For black on cream, you don't even need spot color. Standard CMYK + K is fine. We’ll punch the warning line in K, text in darker K for contrast.”

Yuna exhales, shoulders dropping half an inch. “Okay. That's the only thing that keeps me up at night: surprise invoices.”

“Copy. You want me to keep you in the lab while this batch spins, or should I send you a preview first?”

“Stay. I trust your hands more than mine right now. And I brought you a candle as thanks, if you don't mind the smell.” She sets a jar on the bench. The umber wax catches the machine’s LED strip, turning it into a warm coin.

“Deal. I’ll run the labels, you watch the cutter tracks. If the registration marks drift, we pause.”

They work in the soft clatter of the platen advancing and the motor’s steady breath. Yuna lines up the first jar, thumbs pressing the label flat along the curve, bubbles escaping like tiny secrets. Jericho checks the alignment, nudges the cutter head half a millimeter, and nods.

“Perfect. Go.”

“Noted.” He could hear the faint hum of traffic behind her words. “I’ll stay on while you run the first loop so I can troubleshoot if a section drops out.”  

Ariadne clipped the first LED cluster to the third bar, twisted the green wire, and stepped back. The tiny globes threw pale gold on the brickwork, turning soot into amber. She aimed her phone’s flashlight along the line; no shadows where there shouldn’t be.  

“Hold the strand here—left hand, two inches below the joint. I’m counting the sections.” Yvon’s voice was calm metronome. “One, two, three—good. Four is dim?”  

She lifted the fourth cluster; a tiny solder joint had cracked during shipping. “It’s flickering.”  

“Pull the two ends apart just enough to see the trace, tin them with the iron, and twist back. Quick; don’t melt the silicone.”  

Hands steady now, she worked. When the light steadied, she exhaled.  

“Nice.” Yvon’s voice softened. “You’ve got calluses on your index finger; keep the pliers vertical when you crimp, it saves the nail.”  

“I’ll try not to maim myself.” She tied off the last loop. The whole railing wore a clean, even line of light, tinsel hanging in precise, icicle-thin drops. No drool, no glare, no exposed

“Wouldn’t dream of it. What’s the time?”  

“Half past six. I need this done before the pizza arrives and she notices I’m doing a craft project instead of, you know, existing socially.”  

“Then start with the splice. I’ll talk you through the heat gun.”  

Ariadne knelt on the frosty concrete, phone wedged under a brick, fingers fumbling with the tiny LED pack. Yvon’s voice guided her: “Hold the shrink tube near the cut, not on the copper; you’ll burn the insulation.”  

“On it. Wait—did I mention the wind?”  

“Wrap the bundle tight; tension is your friend.”  

She twisted wire, sealed the cut, and snapped the strand back to life. Ten bulbs blinked white, then steady. The balcony above stayed dark; her roommate had forgotten the date. Ariadne smiled despite herself.  

“Fixed,” she said. “Now the tinsel.”  

“Copper core, garden wire, lash every six inches. And Ariadne?”  

“Yeah?”  

“Leave one small gap in the middle. It’ll look more natural, like a real icicle formation. You’re not trying to build a light bar; you’re building winter.”  

She paused, then nodded at the empty air. “Winter. Got it.”

Wilma blinked, then laughed. “Oh, honey, that was your machine’s tension talking, not the tape. But fine—skip it. If the mouth still won’t sit right, we’ll stay-stitch a bias strip instead. No tape, promise.”

Yona relaxed, shoulders dropping an inch. “Thanks. I’ll test all trims first. I love that thing about fabric being neighbors—sewing is just urban planning.”

“Sewing is negotiation,” Wilma corrected, tapping the guide. “You propose, the cloth counters. You get a yes by being reasonable and thorough.”

Yona flipped the page. “Okay. So I’ll cut my sari silk panel a touch smaller to account for relaxation, stay-stitch the linen bib, interface the pocket mouths, and I’ll pretend seam tape doesn’t exist. And when the corduroy wrangles me, I’ll remember you’re watching.”

“Always. And if the Bernina begins to sound like a tractor, unplug it, show me the bobbin case, and don’t panic.”

“Wouldn’t dream of it.”

The bus engine rumbled faintly down the street, a low growl that vibrated the window sash. Yona closed the notebook, pencil clicking into place. “I’ll bring you the finished thing. And a last chapter. If you’ll promise not to critique my hemline.”

Wilma’s hands went still over the tin. A beat passed. Then she laughed, a dry sound like pages turning. “You’re the second person this week to forbid me. Third if you count my reflection.”

Yona grinned, shoulders dropping. “I’ll buy you coffee if you promise not to bring tape into this project.”

“Coffee’s a bribe, but I’ll take it. You’ll earn it the moment you hand-me a thread that isn’t nylon.”

They set to work. Scissors sang against linen. Pins clinked into the pincushion like rain. Wilma adjusted the presser foot, eyed the feed dogs, and started the machine. It purred, then coughed, then settled into a steady rhythm. Yona watched the seam roll out, clean and even, and felt something unclench in her chest she hadn’t noticed was tight.

“Why aprons?” Wilma asked, not looking up.

“Because they hold the day together,” Yona said. “And because I want to make something that lasts longer than me.”

Wilma’s hands didn’t miss a stitch. “Then let it. Cut the bias tape generous—aprons get washed and washed. Life does that to cloth. And to people.”
